progress_impact.note: Parallel non-blocking. Stage 4 remains primary (Pass 4.3 next). Dials unchanged at Validation 33 / Overall 83 / Unabridged 100.

success_test: A skeptical 17-year-old and a political-economy professor should both be able to read the same page—the first understands it, and the second recognizes that we have not trivialized the ideas.

opening.eyebrow: Flagship public understanding · 30–60 minute guided journey
opening.title: What is Constitutional Capitalism?
opening.lede: Not a vocabulary card. An intellectual journey: feel the differences between systems, watch incentives change, and see exactly what Constitutional Capitalism is—and is not.

arkansas_open.label: ILLUSTRATION
arkansas_open.text: Imagine a poultry processing plant near a small Arkansas town. Farmers supply under contract. Workers clock in. Trucks leave for national buyers. A bank holds loans. Someone claims residual profit. The county watches taxes and road wear. That one plant already contains markets, ownership, labor, capital, power, and public rules. Different philosophies answer differently—before they ever use their labels.

choose_society.title: Choose the society you want to build
choose_society.intro: Questions first. Labels later. Pick an answer; then see how traditions tend to reason.

questions.prompt: A town's only hospital is closing. What should happen?

choices.label: Let the market decide—if it cannot survive, it closes
Public ownership or heavy subsidy to keep doors open
Regulate + finance access while keeping mixed ownership options
Test function: access, outcomes, household burden, competition—then choose the least-dominating tool that works

traditions.Laissez-faire: Prefer exit and private alternatives; fear permanent political capture of healthcare capital.
traditions.Socialism: Essential care should not depend on residual private claims; socialize or democratize the facility.
traditions.Social democracy: Keep markets where useful; guarantee access through public finance and regulation.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: Hospital function is essential. Ownership is not slogan-first. Measure household access and capture risk; public ownership only if it clears purpose, Role Conflict, and evidence.

questions.prompt: A company controls 80% of the state's poultry processing capacity. Should government intervene?

choices.label: No—scale is efficiency
Break it up or nationalize
Regulate pricing and labor standards
Measure scale benefits AND power harms (prices, entry, monopsony, politics) before choosing a tool

traditions.Laissez-faire: Prefer contestability and entry; antitrust only for clear predation.
traditions.Progressive / antitrust: Concentration itself can be a public problem—antitrust as countervailing power.
traditions.Socialism: Worker/public control of the essential processing chain.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: Size is not automatically vice. Unaccountable market power and political capture are. Extraction Test + competition policy before ideology.

questions.prompt: AI doubles productivity but eliminates thousands of jobs. Who should benefit from the productivity increase?

choices.label: Whoever owns the capital that deployed the AI
Society as a whole via public ownership of AI capital
Workers and households via taxes, training, and transfers
Trace ownership, risk, surplus, and household agency—then design claims without killing discovery

traditions.Market capitalism: Residual claims follow capital risk; labor markets adjust; growth raises living standards over time.
traditions.Socialism: Socialize the means that produce the surplus; do not leave AI rents to private capital alone.
traditions.Social democracy: Keep private AI firms; tax and retrain; protect households from transition shocks.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: Productivity is not prosperity until households can retain money, build assets, and keep agency. Ask who owns the AI stack and where surplus lands.

questions.prompt: Arkansas discovers a valuable natural resource. Who should own the upside?

choices.label: Whoever holds the private mineral rights
The public, via state ownership of extraction
Private extraction + royalties/taxes funding services
Public claim proportional to public resource/risk—then intergenerational rules (not binge spending)

traditions.Georgism: Land/resource rents are uniquely social; capture them for the commons.
traditions.Norway-style social market: Public resource claim + disciplined sovereign investment abroad.
traditions.Laissez-faire: Secure private rights; tax lightly; let markets allocate.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: BORROW intergenerational treatment of exhaustible wealth. REJECT pretending Arkansas is Norway. QUESTION which Arkansas assets actually have rent characteristics.

questions.prompt: A family works full-time but cannot build savings because housing, healthcare, transportation and childcare consume nearly everything. Is that household prosperous?

choices.label: Yes if GDP and employment are rising
No—decommodify essentials via public provision
No—raise wages and expand transfers
No—Household Prosperity Surplus is the unit of success, not GDP

traditions.Growth-first: Rising output eventually lifts boats; focus on productivity.
traditions.Social democracy: Market wages plus welfare state make life livable.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: If full-time work cannot produce retained surplus and shock buffers, the system is failing that household—regardless of GSP headlines.

questions.prompt: A successful entrepreneur becomes a billionaire. Is that itself a problem?

choices.label: Never—wealth is proof of value created
Yes—extreme wealth should not exist
Only if it buys political power or destroys competition
Wealth is allowed; domination via capture is not

traditions.Libertarian: Peaceful wealth is not aggression; curb state predation first.
traditions.Egalitarian socialist: Extreme wealth concentrates power; tax or restructure.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: People can become extremely wealthy. The constitutional problem begins when wealth purchases the referee.

questions.prompt: A public enterprise earns a profit. Who should receive it?

choices.label: It should not exist—privatize
The general treasury immediately
Reinvest in the enterprise
Only after costs—and only COUNTABLE reserved public cash clears the waterfall

traditions.State capitalism: State firms as national champions; surplus to state strategy.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: Revenue ≠ profit ≠ distributable cash ≠ public cash. COUNTABLE is still $0 because hope is not cash.

questions.prompt: Government can use AI to make benefit decisions faster. Should it?

choices.label: Yes—speed is compassion
No—humans only
Yes with audits
Only with Digital Due Process: notice, review, appeal, audit trail

traditions.Technocracy: Optimize administration; accept some opacity for performance.
traditions.Constitutional Capitalism: AI can enhance capacity. It cannot silently become sovereign. Consequential automation without process FAILED as designed in Pass 4.2.

act1_tensions.title: Act I — What problem are we trying to solve?
act1_tensions.intro: Before Constitutional Capitalism appears, confront the tensions every system must resolve. Every political-economic philosophy is, in part, a different answer to these tensions.

tensions.title: Freedom vs security
tensions.q: How much risk should individuals carry?

tensions.title: Markets vs power
tensions.q: When does successful competition create enough concentration to undermine future competition?

tensions.title: Private ownership vs public purpose
tensions.q: When should ownership remain private, and when—if ever—does public participation make sense?

tensions.title: Local control vs equal rights
tensions.q: How much should communities decide for themselves?

tensions.title: Growth vs inheritance
tensions.q: How much of today's prosperity can legitimately consume tomorrow's resources?

tensions.title: Capital accumulation vs political equality
tensions.q: How wealthy can someone become before wealth starts becoming political power?

tensions.title: Government capacity vs government domination
tensions.q: How capable should the state be without becoming dangerous?

act2_worlds_teaser.title: Act II — Walk through competing answers
act2_worlds_teaser.intro: Philosophies are worlds, not cards. Start with capitalism's bakery-to-power path—then visit socialism and social democracy. Full world-pages deepen next; this flagship keeps the journey moving toward what CC proposes.

capitalism_world.imagine: Imagine you have an idea for a business. You find investors willing to risk their money. You hire workers who voluntarily accept wages. Customers decide whether what you produce is worth buying. If you succeed, you may become wealthy. If you fail, you may lose your investment.
why_powerful: People experiment without asking government permission for every try
capitalism_world.tension: Successful businesses accumulate capital. Capital can buy competitors. Scale lowers costs—and can raise barriers. Ownership compounds. Wealth can influence politics. Workers may depend on employers more than employers depend on any one worker.
capitalism_world.punch: Capitalism's strength—capital accumulation—can eventually become one of capitalism's internal threats if it destroys competition.

other_worlds.name: Socialism
other_worlds.hook: What if productive capital's surplus should not concentrate in private residual claims?

other_worlds.name: Social democracy
other_worlds.hook: Keep markets productive—protect households from insecurity with tax-and-transfer and public services.

other_worlds.name: Libertarianism
other_worlds.hook: Strong rights; minimal state; fear political allocation more than market inequality.

other_worlds.name: Distributism
other_worlds.hook: Spread productive property widely among families—not capitalists or the state alone.

other_worlds.name: Georgism
other_worlds.hook: Socialize land/resource rents; leave produced capital freer.

is_not.title: Act III — So what are we proposing?
is_not.subtitle: First: what Constitutional Capitalism refuses to accept

items.title: Not laissez-faire
items.body: It does not assume every market outcome is automatically legitimate. Markets can fail. Competition can disappear. Costs can be shifted onto people who never agreed to bear them. Wealth can purchase political influence. The state sometimes must act.

items.title: Not socialism
items.body: It does not presume productive property should generally be collectively or publicly owned. Private ownership, private enterprise, entrepreneurship, profit and capital accumulation remain legitimate and essential.

items.title: Not state capitalism
items.body: It does not envision government owning major industries simply because they are economically important. Public ownership has to pass a functional test.

items.title: Not social democracy
items.body: It does not primarily define prosperity as successful market capitalism followed by redistribution through taxation and public services. It asks an earlier question: Who owns the productive assets and who receives the returns before redistribution begins?

items.title: Not communism
items.body: It does not seek abolition of private productive property, markets, profit, or capital accumulation.

items.title: Not protectionism
items.body: It does not assume Arkansas should make everything Arkansas consumes. Trade can make Arkansas richer. The goal is productive retention, not economic isolation.

items.title: Not anti-corporate
items.body: Scale can create efficiencies, innovation and consumer benefit. The problem is not corporate size by itself. The problem is unaccountable market power or political capture.

items.title: Not government by experts
items.body: Experts provide evidence. Citizens remain sovereign.

items.title: Not technocracy
items.body: Measurement informs decisions. It does not replace democracy.

items.title: Not equality of outcomes
items.body: People will make different decisions, possess different abilities, take different risks and achieve different outcomes. The objective is not identical wealth.

items.title: Not a guarantee against failure
items.body: Businesses will fail. Pilots will fail. Programs will fail. The system's obligation is to learn and correct, not promise perfection.

items.title: Not abolish-taxes-first
items.body: Build the bridge before removing the old road. No tax disappears because a spreadsheet says some future system might replace it.

seven_principles.title: Liberty comes first
seven_principles.body: Individuals possess rights that government doesn't grant and cannot casually remove for economic convenience. Economic prosperity does not excuse unlimited state power.

seven_principles.title: Markets are powerful—but they require competition
seven_principles.body: Markets coordinate enormous amounts of information better than central planners generally can. Monopoly, capture, externalities and barriers to entry can prevent markets from functioning as markets. Government acts primarily to protect the conditions of genuine competition, not to substitute itself for every market decision.

seven_principles.title: Ownership matters
seven_principles.body: Two towns can have the same factory, workers, sales and wages—and still have different economies if surplus stays local in one and leaves every year in the other. CC asks constantly: Who owns? Who bears risk? Who controls? Who receives surplus? Where does capital accumulate?

seven_principles.title: The household is the unit of success
seven_principles.body: Not GDP. Not government revenue. Not the stock market. Not average wages alone. Can families retain money, build assets, survive shocks, access essential systems, gain economic agency, own productive capital, and have control over their time? That is why Household Prosperity Surplus matters.

seven_principles.title: Public investment can earn a public return—but only when earned
seven_principles.body: If taxpayers bear risk or supply productive capital, they may sometimes participate in the upside. But revenue ≠ profit ≠ distributable cash ≠ public cash. Public ownership is not the default. The burden of proof remains high. That is exactly why COUNTABLE is still $0—a credibility point, not an embarrassment.

seven_principles.title: Political and economic power must both remain distributed
seven_principles.body: A government powerful enough to control everything can dominate citizens. Private wealth powerful enough to buy government can also dominate citizens. The system tries to prevent both state domination and private capture of the state.

seven_principles.title: Prosperity must compound across generations
seven_principles.body: A generation shouldn't appear prosperous by borrowing from the next, destroying infrastructure, depleting resources, creating unfunded obligations, or consuming assets future Arkansans need. Final accounting: Did we leave the next generation more capable than we found ourselves?

twenty_questions.sec5: Wealth from peaceful production and voluntary exchange is legitimate. The constitutional problem begins when wealth purchases the referee, blocks entry, or converts market success into political domination.
Scale can serve households through lower costs and innovation. Size is not the offense. Unaccountable market power and capture are.

Only when function, risk, capital source, competition, and public purpose justify it—and after Role Conflict walls. Pass 4.1 killed public ownership as default; Pass 4.2 killed guarantee-heavy designs under Art. 16 §1.

twenty_questions.q: Does everyone receive the same income?
twenty_questions.sec5: Equal standing under law is not identical outcomes. The test is household agency and anti-domination—not forced equality of wealth.
CC cares whether households can earn, retain, and build. Job guarantees are a policy tool requiring separate evidence—not a definitional requirement.
It seeks to reduce dependence on extractive taxation only after proven replacement exists. Near-term dual abolition FAILED under Pass 4.1. Build the bridge before removing the old road.
The test is access, outcomes, market function, household burden, and resilience—not a single ownership slogan.
Private productive ownership, markets, profit, and capital accumulation remain essential. Socialism generally socializes productive claims; CC does not.
Markets and private enterprise are load-bearing. Competition protection, anti-capture, ownership analysis, and household metrics modify pure laissez-faire.
Profit is a signal and residual claim for risk-bearing. The question is whether competition and rights remain intact—and where surplus accumulates.
Inheritance is part of family capital formation. Any tax architecture that eventually survives validation is Stage 4 / legislative work—not a slogan.
Intervention needs a specific market-failure or essential-system justification—not a preference for political allocation.

twenty_questions.sec30: It values local productive capacity—rejects retention-at-any-cost.
twenty_questions.sec5: Pass 4.1 required a counterfactual price/quality/capacity test. Productive retention ≠ autarky.
Trade can enrich Arkansas. The issue is leakage of surplus and agency without compensatory capacity—not borders as destiny.

twenty_questions.sec30: No singular labor institution is mandatory.
twenty_questions.sec5: Worker voice, ownership, and bargaining are tools evaluated by household and competition effects—not loyalty to one form.

twenty_questions.sec30: AI can enhance capacity; it cannot silently become sovereign.
twenty_questions.sec5: Pass 4.2: consequential automation without Digital Due Process FAILED as designed.

twenty_questions.q: What happens when an idea fails?
twenty_questions.sec5: Stage 4 is publicly trying to prove claims wrong. Failed propositions are progress when removed for good reasons.

twenty_questions.q: Who decides whether the system is working?
twenty_questions.sec30: Evidence informs; democratic institutions and citizens govern.
twenty_questions.sec5: Experts are not sovereign. Dashboards do not replace elections or rights.

twenty_questions.sec30: Reserved public cash that cleared the evidence waterfall—not hoped-for revenue.
twenty_questions.sec5: COUNTABLE remains $0 after Pass 4.1. That is a successful research result if evidence does not clear.

twenty_questions.sec30: Household prosperity, liberty, resilient communities, and greater inheritance for the next generation.
twenty_questions.sec5: Not GDP theater. Not government revenue theater. Capability compounding under constitutional constraint.

liberty_town.title: One town, five systems
liberty_town.label: ILLUSTRATION
liberty_town.name: Liberty, Arkansas
liberty_town.intro: A clearly fictional town. Same people, same geography—different institutional answers. Not a utopian simulator.
questions: What happens when the factory closes?
How does the town attract capital?

answers.What happens when the factory closes?: Labor and capital reallocate; town absorbs shock

answers.Who owns the hospital?: Often public or heavily publicly financed access
answers.Who decides electric rates?: Regulated utility with social tariffs possible
answers.How does the town attract capital?: Skills, infrastructure, stable rules + welfare floor

answers.Who owns the hospital?: Function test—private, nonprofit, or public if earned
answers.Who finances housing?: Private markets + targeted public tools; no fake COUNTABLE
answers.Who decides electric rates?: Utility rules with Role Conflict walls if public participates
answers.What happens when the factory closes?: Household buffers + competition for new capital; no guarantee theater
answers.Who provides retirement security?: Mixed; federal constraints mapped in Pass 4.2
answers.How is education funded?: Current legal baseline; residency pricing differentials lawful with care
answers.What happens to profits?: Follow ownership/risk; public share only after waterfall
answers.What happens when monopoly emerges?: Measure power harms; antitrust / entry / least-dominating tool

household_map.title: Stand in the middle of the system

laissez.name: Laissez-faire capitalism
laissez.summary: Private residual claims dominate. Government is night-watchman-ish. Household risk is high; discovery is high.

socdem.name: Social democracy
socdem.summary: Private production + large tax-financed services and transfers. Household risk buffered after market outcomes.

socialism.name: Socialism
socialism.summary: Social claims on productive surplus. Markets may exist but ownership of capital is the core fight.

statecap.name: State capitalism
statecap.summary: State as owner-strategist. Households secondary to national projects.

cc.name: Constitutional Capitalism
cc.summary: Household at center. Markets + ownership geography + anti-capture + COUNTABLE honesty. Public play only when earned.
cc.surplus: Follow ownership/risk; public only after waterfall
cc.government: Protect competition and rights; limited functional ownership

stage4_attack.title: We are trying to prove ourselves wrong
stage4_attack.intro: Stage 4 is hostile validation. Most political projects hide failed assumptions. We publish them.

survived: Statutory IIT pathway (legality ≠ near-term fiscal clearance)
failed: Dual IIT + property abolition under Base@16y stacks (Pass 4.1)
changed: Tax-transition talk must carry ~$7.23B replacement burden map
Local pilots mapped on a legal ladder (not pure autonomy fiction)
Procurement redesigned as lawful toolkit, not ideology
unknown: Any feeder that honestly clears COUNTABLE

featured_claim.claim: Arkansas could eventually eliminate personal income and property taxes.
featured_claim.hoped: Alternative public-income mechanisms might replace them.
featured_claim.found: Current replacement burden roughly $7.23B (IIT + layered property map).
featured_claim.changed: Dual abolition cannot proceed without independently proven replacement capacity.

misconceptions.a: No. Private productive ownership, markets, profit, and capital accumulation remain essential. CC asks who owns and where surplus goes—without socializing productive property as the default answer.
No. Public ownership is not default. It must clear function, evidence, Role Conflict, and—after Pass 4.2—avoid illegal private debt guarantees.
No. Abolish-taxes-first is explicitly rejected. Build the bridge before removing the old road. Pass 4.1 kept COUNTABLE at $0.
Norway is a World Lab case to BORROW intergenerational resource discipline—not to copy petroleum economics onto Arkansas. See NON-LESSON rules.

misconceptions.q: This is just capitalism with welfare.
misconceptions.a: Social democracy prioritizes post-market redistribution. CC asks an earlier ownership and surplus question—and treats capture of the referee as constitutional failure.
CC shares rights seriousness and market respect, but rejects the claim that every market outcome is automatically legitimate or that anti-capture tools are optional.

misconceptions.q: Why not just call it social democracy?
misconceptions.a: Because ownership-before-redistribution, COUNTABLE discipline, and dual anti-domination (state and private) are not optional branding—they change the architecture.
It can become that—which is why public ownership is not default, why the waterfall exists, and why Stage 4 attacks the claim.

misconceptions.q: What stops this from becoming authoritarian?
misconceptions.a: Constitutional rights floors, distributed power, Digital Due Process, Role Conflict tests, and democratic sovereignty over experts. Capacity without domination is the design problem.

misconceptions.q: Who pays for all of this?
misconceptions.a: Whoever the transparent incidence map says—plus opportunity cost. No teleported cash. COUNTABLE remains $0 until evidence clears.

misconceptions.q: What if your numbers are wrong?
misconceptions.a: Then the proposal changes. That is the culture Stage 4 is building.

challenges.serious: Public-choice incentives, information problems, and historical failures are real.
challenges.cc_answer: We agree this is a core risk. That is why public ownership is not default; why Role Conflict walls exist; why the public-income waterfall refuses hoped-for cash; and why Stage 4 keeps attacking.
challenges.satisfaction: Partially / unresolved—Pass 4.3–4.5 will keep pressing behavior, resilience, and capture.

challenges.objection: This will just become another tax-and-spend program.
challenges.serious: Political systems drift toward spending without productive returns.
challenges.cc_answer: Dependency Rule and Replacement Readiness exist to prevent abolish-or-spend theater. Pass 4.1 already failed near-term replacement fantasies.
challenges.satisfaction: Architecture survived; clearance did not—honesty over marketing.

challenges.serious: Any dashboard can be selectively framed.
challenges.cc_answer: Comprehensible Government and anti-manipulation rules are Stage 4/5 work (OV-35-06). Metrics inform; they do not replace rights or elections.
